title: Goodbye, Michael

jokes.text: Michael narrates about moving to Colorado, 'just up here getting used to the altitude' while presumably doing something mundane in the office
jokes.setup: Michael announces his big life change — moving to Colorado
jokes.punchline: 'Just up here getting used to the altitude' — a completely meaningless, grandiose non-preparation delivered with total sincerity
jokes.explanation: Strong character comedy because only Michael would 'prepare' for altitude by imagining himself already there. The absurd logic is perfectly Michael — confident, meaningless action. Sets the tone for the episode beautifully.

jokes.text: Dwight reveals the 'Rocky Mountain oysters' he fed Michael are bull testicles he 'cut off fresh this morning'
jokes.setup: Dwight presents Michael with a Colorado specialty treat, acting like a 'butler'
jokes.punchline: They're bull testicles — and Dwight cut them off fresh that morning, implying he mutilated an animal as a revenge prank
jokes.explanation: The 'fresh this morning' detail is what elevates this. It's not just a prank — Dwight implies he butchered an animal specifically for this. Perfect Dwight escalation. The callback to his beet farm/farm animal context makes it earned rather than random gross-out.

jokes.text: Michael: 'After what you did, you expect to be buttled?' / Dwight: 'After you didn't recommend me?'
jokes.setup: Michael is outraged that Dwight pranked him
jokes.punchline: Michael invents the verb 'buttled' (to be served as a butler) completely naturally, and the argument reveals this whole prank stems from Michael not recommending Dwight for his job
jokes.explanation: 'Buttled' is a wonderful Michael-ism — he creates neologisms without realizing it, and it works perfectly. The reveal that Dwight's prank is rooted in genuine hurt feelings adds emotional texture while staying funny. High character integration.

jokes.text: Michael: 'I was just thinking maybe I should keep a salami in my pocket... in order to feed the bears.'
jokes.setup: Michael asks Dwight for bear safety advice in the Rockies
jokes.punchline: Michael's plan is to carry salami in his pocket to feed bears — the logic being friendly and generous, the reality being suicidal
jokes.explanation: Quintessential Michael Scott logic — generosity applied to a scenario where it's catastrophically wrong. The pause before 'in order to feed the bears' is perfectly structured. Only Michael would think carrying meat near wildlife is a kindness plan.

jokes.text: Dwight's escalating bear lecture: 'Black bears can smell a salami at five miles... they run faster than a horse. So if you were thinking about outrunning them on a horse, I would try a cheetah.'
jokes.setup: Dwight is genuinely trying to warn Michael about bear danger
jokes.punchline: Dwight's advice escalates into the absurd suggestion of outrunning a bear on a cheetah — delivered with complete deadpan sincerity as practical wilderness guidance
jokes.explanation: This is exceptional Dwight comedy. The escalation from accurate wilderness knowledge ('they run faster than a horse') to the deadpan absurdity of recommending a cheetah is perfectly structured. Dwight's character requires him to be simultaneously the most competent and most ridiculous person in any room — this nails it. The structure is impeccable: accurate premise → logical extension → impossible conclusion, all delivered without a wink. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor in quality.

jokes.text: 'You in tight pants, Michael, are a salami to a black bear.'
jokes.setup: Dwight has been warning Michael about bears smelling meat
jokes.punchline: Dwight summarizes by comparing Michael himself — in tight pants — to a giant salami, making Michael's body the bait
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — it synthesizes the whole bear conversation into one devastating image. 'In tight pants' is a beautiful specific detail that makes it visual and physical. Highly quotable, builds on the escalation, and lands as the cap to a strong comedic sequence. The callback structure is clean.

jokes.text: Michael: 'Okay, so no salami in the pants. How about a pepperoni?' / Dwight: 'Any kind of meat you can possibly name.'
jokes.setup: Dwight has just finished warning Michael that any meat will attract bears
jokes.punchline: Michael immediately pivots to asking about pepperoni, missing the entire point — and Dwight has to explicitly say 'any meat'
jokes.explanation: The button on the bear sequence. Michael's inability to learn even one obvious lesson in real time is perfect character comedy. The specificity of 'pepperoni' rather than a generic follow-up makes it funnier — it's not random, it's Michael thinking he found a clever workaround.

jokes.text: Jim tells Michael he doesn't have a desk to put his toys on since he has no job lined up, then casually asks if he can have Michael's toy truck
jokes.setup: Jim is helping Michael pack up his office and makes a cutting practical observation about Michael's lack of future employment
jokes.punchline: Having just reminded Michael of his precarious situation, Jim immediately asks for the toy truck — his real motivation revealed
jokes.explanation: Effective cringe comedy — Jim's real-talk about Michael having no job is slightly mean, then his ask for the truck reveals the veiled self-interest. The emotional layers (this is also genuinely sad) are what make Office comedy work at its best.

jokes.text: Michael confessional: 'I don't leave till tomorrow, so tomorrow I will be a wreck.'
jokes.setup: Michael is asked if he's sad
jokes.punchline: He insists he's fine today — he's already planned exactly when he'll fall apart, with complete confidence in his future emotional breakdown
jokes.explanation: Michael schedules his emotional breakdown like a meeting. This is deeply character-specific — his emotional immaturity expressed through his office-manager mindset of planning and controlling everything, including grief. Excellent economy.

jokes.text: Gabe confronts Erin: 'I've seen some horrible things. I own over 200 horror movies.'
jokes.setup: Gabe is trying to intimidate Erin, saying she doesn't want to get on his bad side
jokes.punchline: His proof of being dangerous/having seen horror is that he owns a horror movie collection — the most passive, nerdy possible credential
jokes.explanation: Perfect character comedy for Gabe — tall, creepy, completely unthreatening. The joke works because 'I own over 200 horror movies' as a threat is so specifically pathetic it could only come from this exact character. It simultaneously lampoons his attempt at intimidation while revealing his actual personality. High quotability and character integration score justified.

jokes.text: Dwight spots Jim in the hallway and says only 'Hi, Tuna.' — Jim's reaction to camera
jokes.setup: Dwight passes Jim in the hallway
jokes.punchline: Dwight uses Jim's old nickname 'Tuna' — a callback to their long history — and Jim presumably gives a tired/bemused look to camera
jokes.explanation: A brief but warm long-running gag callback. Works on familiarity and the implied camera look from Jim. Nothing structurally complex but earned by the show's history.

jokes.text: Kevin, apparently caught on camera going to the bathroom, says 'You guys are filming people when they go to the bathroom now?'
jokes.setup: Kevin appears during what seems to be a mundane scene
jokes.punchline: Kevin breaks the documentary frame to complain about the camera crew's intrusion into bathrooms — suggesting either he was filmed or he assumed he was being filmed in embarrassing circumstances
jokes.explanation: Functional meta-joke about the documentary format. Kevin's oblivious self-incrimination (why does he assume he was filmed in the bathroom?) is the best part. Moderate craft.

jokes.text: 'The dream team and Meredith.' — said after listing Angela, Phyllis, and Pam as the 'dream team' party planners
jokes.setup: Michael greets the party planning committee, calling them 'the dream team'
jokes.punchline: He then adds 'and Meredith' — as a clear afterthought, implicitly excluding her from the dream team designation
jokes.explanation: Clean comic structure with Michael's thoughtless cruelty on full display. The timing — saying 'the dream team' then catching himself and adding Meredith as an afterthought — is a perfect pause beat. Economical and character-specific.

jokes.text: Michael says he wants vanilla ice cream so 'everybody will like it' after being told mint chocolate chip is his favorite
jokes.setup: The committee announces mint chocolate chip — Michael's favorite — for the party
jokes.punchline: Michael, at his own goodbye party, overrides his own favorite flavor to get something 'everybody will like' — self-denial as a form of managerial performance on his last day
jokes.explanation: A subtle character joke — Michael's need to be liked overrides even his own desires. The irony that they got his favorite specifically for him and he vetoes it is bittersweet-funny. Understated.

jokes.text: Michael's talking head: Shows the mug he bought himself, then the 'World's Best Boss' mug that was given to him (implied). 'I still need something to drink out of, though.'
jokes.setup: Michael displays gifts and belongings he's packing — including his iconic 'World's Best Boss' mug that he famously bought for himself
jokes.punchline: He acknowledges he bought that mug for himself, someone else gave him a mug, but he still needs something to drink out of — the punchline being the absurdity of needing a third mug or the implication the gifted mug isn't good enough
jokes.explanation: Relies heavily on audience familiarity with the iconic mug gag. The payoff is a bit muddled in the transcript — clearer visually than in text. Moderate craft.

jokes.text: Michael builds up to a 20-year secret about Phyllis: 'When Phyllis was in high school, she was so cute.' Long pause. 'And she still is.'
jokes.setup: Michael announces he'll reveal a secret he's kept for over 20 years about Phyllis — everyone braces for something scandalous
jokes.punchline: The 'secret' is just that Phyllis was cute in high school — and still is. Completely harmless and devoid of content.
jokes.explanation: Excellent misdirection structure — the setup generates enormous expectation (20 years! A secret!) and the anticlimax is perfectly calibrated to Michael's character. He genuinely thinks this is a meaningful revelation. The timing of the pause before 'and she still is' is crucial.

jokes.text: Phyllis confessional: 'I thought he knew about the baby I gave away.'
jokes.setup: Michael just delivered his anticlimactic 'secret' about Phyllis being cute in high school
jokes.punchline: Phyllis reveals she has an actual scandalous secret — a baby she gave away — and was terrified Michael was about to reveal it
jokes.explanation: This is one of the best jokes in the episode. It's the perfect tag on the misdirection sequence — Michael's anticlimactic 'secret' is immediately followed by Phyllis revealing she has a REAL dark secret that she was terrified about. The economy is extraordinary — one sentence flips the entire joke on its head, adds a completely unexpected dark dimension to Phyllis's character, and gets a huge laugh. The structure is near-perfect: setup builds expectation, Michael deflates it, Phyllis re-inflates it with something much darker. Earns its high score.

jokes.text: Pam presents Michael with nearly-unfinished mittens that cannot be wet, dry-cleaned, or hand-washed with water — the instructions making them effectively un-cleanable
jokes.setup: Pam gives Michael going-away mittens she's been knitting
jokes.punchline: The care instructions are an accumulating comedy of errors — they can't be dry-cleaned, can't get wet, must be 'hand washed without water' — making the gift essentially unwearable and unmaintainable
jokes.explanation: 'Hand washed without water' is the key absurdist escalation that makes this work. Each instruction makes the previous one worse. Good escalating comedy structure in a relatively brief bit.

jokes.text: Michael: 'Sounds great. I just think it's great.' — accepting the unwearable mittens with complete sincerity
jokes.setup: Pam has just explained that the mittens are essentially impossible to care for
jokes.punchline: Michael's enthusiastic double acceptance ('sounds great... just think it's great') shows he either didn't process the instructions or doesn't care — pure Michael obliviousness
jokes.explanation: A good button on the mitten bit. Michael's double 'great' suggests he stopped listening halfway through. Functional character moment.

jokes.text: Michael gives Stanley his 'felt' — a single piece of felt — saying 'may you never lose the fun-loving quality in life'
jokes.setup: Michael is giving meaningful going-away gifts to staff; he builds up 'bestowing' something on Stanley who loves puzzles
jokes.punchline: The gift is a single piece of felt, accompanied by an ironic wish for Stanley to keep his 'fun-loving quality' — Stanley, famously the least fun-loving person in the office
jokes.explanation: The double joke here: (1) the absurdity of felt as a going-away gift, and (2) wishing the perpetually miserable Stanley to keep his 'fun-loving quality.' Michael either doesn't know Stanley at all or genuinely thinks this is meaningful. Both readings are funny.

jokes.text: Stanley: 'Where's the rest of it? It's got no balls.'
jokes.setup: Michael has just given Stanley a piece of felt with great ceremony
jokes.punchline: Stanley, apparently expecting a full felt board or toy, notes the gift is incomplete and anatomically deficient — delivered with Stanley's signature total deadpan
jokes.explanation: Stanley's complete disdain for the gift, expressed through what sounds like a complaint about a feltboard missing pieces, is perfect. 'It's got no balls' is gloriously ambiguous and delivered with Stanley's signature zero-investment deadpan. Short, sharp, characterful.

jokes.text: Michael gives Andy his top 10 client accounts, saying Andy 'needs confidence that he is a great salesman' — Andy immediately says 'You know I'm the worst salesman here, right?'
jokes.setup: Michael builds up to giving Andy something meaningful — his ten most important accounts
jokes.punchline: Andy's immediate self-aware confession that he's the worst salesman completely deflates Michael's grand gesture
jokes.explanation: Good structural joke — Michael's heartfelt buildup is punctured by Andy's honest self-assessment. The exchange that follows (Michael: 'You sold us all on Andy. A product nobody wanted.') extends it well.

jokes.text: Michael: 'But you're the best salesman on the inside.' Andy: 'What does that even mean?' Michael: 'You sold us all on Andy. A product that nobody wanted.'
jokes.setup: Michael is trying to inspire Andy despite Andy's accurate self-assessment
jokes.punchline: 'You sold us all on Andy. A product that nobody wanted.' — Michael intends this as a compliment, delivering it as the world's most backhanded endorsement
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best lines. Michael means it sincerely as encouragement, which makes it the ultimate unintentional insult. 'A product that nobody wanted' is devastating and hilarious — it accidentally captures how Andy is perceived in the office. The structure is perfect: earnest metaphor → apparent compliment → devastating subtext. Highly quotable, great character integration for both Michael (oblivious warmth) and Andy (hapless sales rep).

jokes.text: Dwight confessional continues: 'I used to be obese. Once you've conquered obesity, everything else is easy. Life literally moves in slow motion.'
jokes.setup: Dwight is rationalizing his loss of the client accounts
jokes.punchline: Dwight pivots from business frustration to a completely non-sequitur claim about having conquered obesity — presented as genuine wisdom, with the absurd follow-up that life moves in slow motion
jokes.explanation: The non-sequitur pivot is classic Dwight confessional style — he'll say something completely unrelated to what was being discussed and present it as relevant insight. 'Life literally moves in slow motion' after 'conquered obesity' is the absurdist peak. Reveals Dwight's grandiose self-image.

jokes.text: Dwight confessional: 'I'm not saying I'm Superman, but let me just put it this way — if I were shot in the head, I'm pretty sure everything would be fine. I almost welcome it.'
jokes.setup: Dwight is continuing his confessional about his invincibility after conquering obesity
jokes.punchline: 'I almost welcome it' — Dwight's grandiosity has escalated to claiming he's bulletproof and slightly inviting assassination to prove it
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'I'm not saying I'm Superman' (but clearly saying it) to 'I almost welcome' being shot in the head is darkly brilliant. The qualifier 'I'm not saying I'm Superman' is immediately contradicted by everything else. 'I almost welcome it' has the cadence of a man who has thought deeply about this. Peak Dwight grandiosity — only this character would frame potential assassination as a confidence-builder.

jokes.text: Michael gives Kevin a gift — a caricature of Kevin. Reacts with recognition, then Michael tears it up saying 'Don't be a caricature, Kevin. Never be a caricature.'
jokes.setup: Michael has a gift for Kevin — it appears to be a flattering caricature (presumably exaggerating Kevin's most prominent features)
jokes.punchline: Michael tears the caricature up and delivers the advice 'Don't be a caricature' — the meta-joke being that Kevin IS essentially a caricature of a person, and this is simultaneously absurd life advice and accidentally profound
jokes.explanation: Inspired bit. The physical gag of getting a caricature only to have it immediately destroyed, combined with 'Don't be a caricature' as sincere life advice, is both absurd and oddly moving. The meta-layer — Kevin is functionally a caricature of a person — gives this more depth than most physical gags. Michael tearing up the drawing while making eye contact to deliver the lesson is great staging.

jokes.text: Michael to Kevin: 'You will be thin. You won't drool over pizza like an animal anymore. You will find love.'
jokes.setup: Michael is giving Kevin an inspirational pep talk about his potential
jokes.punchline: Michael's encouragement inadvertently catalogs all of Kevin's worst qualities — drooling over pizza 'like an animal,' being overweight, being unloved — while claiming he'll transcend them
jokes.explanation: 'You won't drool over pizza like an animal anymore' is the standout line — specific, visual, simultaneously insulting and hopeful. Michael's inspirational speeches that document failings rather than inspire are a classic Michael move. Character-specific and well-executed.

jokes.text: Kevin: 'Michael, I'm pretty much okay with who I am now.' Michael: 'Don't be. You should never settle for who you are.'
jokes.setup: Kevin pushes back on Michael's harsh inspirational speech with genuine self-acceptance
jokes.punchline: Michael's response — 'Don't be. You should never settle for who you are' — is meant to be encouraging but is the most casually devastating possible reply to someone expressing self-acceptance
jokes.explanation: 'You should never settle for who you are' is a deeply quotable, perfectly constructed line that works on multiple levels: (1) it's accidentally anti-self-help philosophy, (2) Michael genuinely means it as inspiration, (3) it's objectively terrible advice, and (4) it's also kind of right in Kevin's specific case. The economy is exceptional — it condenses Michael's oblivious cruelty-as-kindness into one sentence. Among the best lines of the episode.

jokes.text: Andy bursts in to interrupt Michael's moment with Oscar: 'Michael, I just lost Porter Hardware!'
jokes.setup: Michael is building to an emotional moment with Oscar, starting 'Oscar, Oscar, Oscar...'
jokes.punchline: Andy crashes in with a work emergency, completely shattering the emotional build — and Michael just tells him 'do your best, buddy' and moves on
jokes.explanation: Works as a callback payoff — Andy immediately loses a client after being given the accounts. The timing punctuates Michael's grand gesture with instant consequences. Michael's breezy 'do your best, buddy' dismissal is characterful.

jokes.text: Michael gives Oscar a 'Scarecrow' diploma he made by hand — Oscar's talking head: 'It looks like it was made by a two-year-old monkey on a farm.'
jokes.setup: Michael calls Oscar his 'Scarecrow' who gave him a brain, and presents him with a handmade diploma
jokes.punchline: Oscar's confessional reveals the diploma looks like it was made by 'a two-year-old monkey on a farm' — a devastatingly specific insult for what is clearly a deeply amateur craft project
jokes.explanation: 'Two-year-old monkey on a farm' is a wonderfully specific insult — not just 'badly made,' but the specificity of the monkey's age and rural setting makes it absurdly precise. Oscar's exacting intellectual standards meeting Michael's crayon-level craft is perfect character clash.

jokes.text: Oscar's confessional, moved despite himself: 'And he just... he just accepted it... that I put all this work into it. He has the lowest opinion of me of anybody.'
jokes.setup: Oscar just criticized the diploma as monkey-made, but watches Michael be genuinely moved by Oscar's acceptance of the gift
jokes.punchline: Oscar is clearly touched — but frames it in terms of Michael having 'the lowest opinion of him' — as if being given a child's art project means Michael doesn't respect him. The joke is that Oscar is emotionally moved while refusing to admit it.
jokes.explanation: Bittersweet Office comedy at its best — Oscar is genuinely moved but can only articulate it through intellectual grievance ('lowest opinion of me'). The gap between Oscar's stated response and his obvious emotion is the joke. This kind of layered character moment is what separates The Office from lesser cringe comedies.

jokes.text: Michael to Oscar: 'Was it just me, or did you think we were gonna have sex at some point?' Oscar: 'It was just you.' Michael: 'How would you have wanted to do it?'
jokes.setup: Michael and Oscar are having a warm farewell moment
jokes.punchline: Michael asks if Oscar thought they'd ever have sex — and when Oscar firmly says 'it was just you,' Michael immediately follows up with logistics
jokes.explanation: Classic Michael Scott cringe in three beats: (1) inappropriate question out of nowhere, (2) definitive shutdown, (3) Michael's failure to process the shutdown and asking follow-up logistics. 'How would you have wanted to do it?' is the peak — he doesn't hear the rejection, only the possibility. Oscar's 'It was just you' is delivered with the weariness of someone who has accepted his reality. Strong character integration for both.

jokes.text: Oscar showing pictures of the senator 'antiquing... rollerblading.' — Then: 'Who's that guy? / Oh, that's Thomas, Robert's aide.' — Long pause.
jokes.setup: Oscar is proudly showing Michael photos of him and his senator boyfriend doing couple activities
jokes.punchline: A third man keeps appearing in the photos — Thomas, the senator's 'aide' — and the implication (that the senator may be having an affair with his aide) hangs in the air with a pointed pause
jokes.explanation: A quietly devastating joke told entirely in subtext. Michael's 'Hmm' and the pause after learning about 'Thomas' plant a seed of suspicion that will pay off later in the series. The joke is what's NOT said — the camera lingers on Michael's half-realization. Good for rewatch value as foreshadowing comedy.

jokes.text: Michael, asked where to send his last paycheck, says Holly's parents live in 'Mountainton, I think.'
jokes.setup: Pam is trying to get Michael's forwarding address for his final paycheck
jokes.punchline: 'Mountainton' — Michael doesn't know the name of the town where his future in-laws live, and the invented name sounds like a child made it up
jokes.explanation: 'Mountainton' as a place name — vaguely plausible enough to be funny, specific enough to be a joke. Michael's total lack of preparation for his move (no address, no job, no plan) is both funny and slightly sad. Pam's 'sounds beautiful' is a good deadpan button.

jokes.text: Michael walks out after a sales call, stops to tell someone 'Walk away, bitch' — apparently to no one obvious, startling the moment.
jokes.setup: Michael and Deangelo are heading out for a client visit.
jokes.punchline: 'Walk away, bitch' — Michael says this with swagger, apparently psyching himself up or addressing the building/situation, not a person.
jokes.explanation: Mildly funny non-sequitur swagger moment. Works as a character beat but doesn't have much structure or earned payoff. Functional.

jokes.text: Pam's deadpan response to 'Mountainton': 'Sounds beautiful.'
jokes.setup: Michael has just invented a fake-sounding town name for where he's moving
jokes.punchline: Pam plays completely straight, affirming 'Mountainton' sounds beautiful — playing along with Michael's cluelessness rather than challenging it
jokes.explanation: Perfect two-word deadpan button. Pam has learned after seven seasons that the only response to Michael is gentle affirmation. Economy is maximal.

jokes.text: The shredder conversation: Phyllis says it won't shred magazines. Kevin says he knows it's not supposed to. Jim: 'Did you break the shredder, Kevin?' Kevin: 'No. It's just that old shredder sucks.'
jokes.setup: Discussion about getting a new shredder — the old one breaks and won't shred magazines.
jokes.punchline: Kevin's insistence that the shredder 'sucks' while simultaneously admitting he knows you're not supposed to put magazines in it strongly implies he did exactly that — and is covering it up with criticism of the equipment.
jokes.explanation: Kevin breaking the shredder with magazines and then blaming the shredder is a perfectly constructed character joke that requires no explicit statement. The implicit accusation and Kevin's semi-evasive response is textbook Kevin. Character integration is strong.

jokes.text: Michael's sudden existential crisis about moving: 'All the channels are gonna be different there. I'm not gonna be able to find my shows. I'm not going to start improv at level one.'
jokes.setup: Michael is alone in his office, supposed to be packing, when he suddenly panics about moving
jokes.punchline: His fears about a major life move are: cable TV channels, improv comedy class credits, and voting location — all absurdly trivial concerns that escalate into the suggestion he'll cancel everything
jokes.explanation: Brilliant character comedy because these ARE Michael's real fears — not losing his job, not leaving friends, but losing improv class progress and TV channel configurations. 'I'm not going to start improv at level one' is peak Michael Scott — his ego cannot accept returning to beginner status at comedy class. The accumulation of trivial concerns creating a major crisis is perfectly structured and deeply character-specific.

jokes.text: 'I just figured out where I was supposed to go to vote.' — delivered as a major concern about moving to Colorado
jokes.setup: Michael is cataloging his fears about moving
jokes.punchline: His final concern: he just figured out his voting location — after apparently years of not knowing — and now has to learn a new one
jokes.explanation: The final escalation beat in Michael's panic list. The implication that he JUST figured out his voting location (after years) is funny on its own — and now he has to start over. Works as an escalating addition to the crisis sequence.

jokes.text: Michael calls Holly to confirm their town name and hears her voice doing a bit: 'Is something wrong? Are you okay?' Holly: 'No. Just needed to hear your voice.' Holly: 'Oh, you mean this?' [does a voice]
jokes.setup: Michael calls Holly in crisis, needing reassurance
jokes.punchline: Holly immediately turns 'hearing her voice' into a playful bit — doing a funny voice when Michael says he just needed to hear it — showing they speak the same comedy language
jokes.explanation: The joke here is that Holly is Michael's perfect match — she hears his earnest 'I needed to hear your voice' and immediately turns it into a bit. This works as both a laugh and a character statement about why they work together.

jokes.text: Holly (on phone): 'My mom's looking at me like she has no sense of humor. It's a joke.'
jokes.setup: Holly is on the phone with Michael doing voices while her mother watches
jokes.punchline: Holly's aside to her mother — explaining that her weird phone behavior is 'a joke' — reveals a mother who clearly doesn't understand Holly's comedy sensibility, and Holly's awareness of the gap
jokes.explanation: A nice offhand character moment — Holly is weird in a way her family doesn't understand. Brief and efficient.

jokes.text: Toby: 'Well, you know, Michael, I have a brother in Boulder. Rory Flenderson. You should look him up.' — extended pause as Michael ignores this completely.
jokes.setup: Toby is trying to make a connection with Michael on his last day
jokes.punchline: The camera cuts to the next line with 'Okay.' — implying Michael offers zero warmth, completely dismisses Toby's attempt at connection, and likely doesn't even look up
jokes.explanation: Michael's contempt for Toby is a series-long running gag, and on his last day he still can't give Toby a genuine moment. The beat between Toby's vulnerable 'look him up' and the flat 'Okay' is the joke — the silence representing Michael's refusal to acknowledge Toby's humanity even now. High character integration; the gag only works because of seven seasons of build.

jokes.text: Michael gives Kelly a goodbye: 'Kelly? If I just went away right now, would that be the best gift I could give you?' Kelly: 'Yes, please. Please go away and stop using that weird, slow voice.'
jokes.setup: Michael is doing meaningful, slow goodbyes with each employee
jokes.punchline: Kelly's response to Michael's dramatic goodbye style is immediate and devastating — she just wants him to leave and stop with the weird voice
jokes.explanation: Kelly cutting through Michael's sentimental pace with total impatience is good character comedy. 'Stop using that weird, slow voice' lampshades Michael's affectation in a way that's both funny and a little mean. Kelly's lack of sentimentality is perfectly in character.

jokes.text: Michael's transfer of Erin to Andy: 'She was once my girl, and she is your girl now.'
jokes.setup: Michael is doing meaningful handoffs on his last day
jokes.punchline: Michael refers to Erin as 'my girl' and transfers her to Andy like property — with Andy's startled reaction ('Wow. Yeah. This is totally unnecessary.')
jokes.explanation: Michael treating Erin like a possession he can transfer is uncomfortable and funny. Andy's 'totally unnecessary' grounds the absurdity. Michael's paternal relationship with Erin throughout the season makes this both weird and earned.

jokes.text: Andy: 'You're not prone to seizures?' — apropos of nothing, to Erin
jokes.setup: Andy is receiving Erin's 'transfer' from Michael
jokes.punchline: Andy's first question to his 'new girl' is whether she has seizures — a completely random medical concern that reveals his nervous awkwardness
jokes.explanation: Andy's random seizure check is bizarre and funny — the non-sequitur worry of an anxious person. Economy is excellent (five words, big laugh potential). Characteristically Andy in its nervous oddness.

jokes.text: Angela warning about bringing Meredith onto the party planning committee: 'You can't let a street dog into the house.' Then: 'Let's hear her out.'
jokes.setup: Meredith suggests erotic cakes for the party. Angela bristles.
jokes.punchline: 'You can't let a street dog into the house' as a description of Meredith is followed immediately by Pam or another character saying 'let's hear her out' — the juxtaposition of Angela's metaphor with someone's interest in the erotic cake idea.
jokes.explanation: 'Street dog' is a great Angela insult for Meredith — perfectly captures her class anxiety and contempt. Angela's snobbery is consistent and the 'let's hear her out' pivot validates Meredith while undercutting Angela.

jokes.text: Meredith's erotic cake feminist defense: 'The women on these cakes, they're not just guys' fantasies. They have real, full women. It is refreshing.' / Angela: 'Don't turn this into some feminist issue.' / Meredith: 'As a person who buys a lot of erotic cakes, it just feels good to be represented on one.'
jokes.setup: Meredith is defending erotic cakes to skeptical colleagues
jokes.punchline: 'As a person who buys a lot of erotic cakes' — Meredith establishes herself as a regular erotic cake consumer, which (a) is hilarious and (b) makes her feminist argument about representation even more absurd-yet-earnest
jokes.explanation: 'As a person who buys a lot of erotic cakes' is one of the great Meredith lines in the series. The feminist framing — she doesn't just buy erotic cakes, she advocates for body diversity on them — creates an absurdly progressive argument in a completely inappropriate context. Angela's 'don't turn this into a feminist issue' and Meredith's earnest response work perfectly. High character integration (only Meredith has this credential and this politics), high quotability, high craft. One of the episode's best jokes.

jokes.text: Erin: 'I think we should do cupcakes. I am one of the few people who looks hot eating a cupcake.'
jokes.setup: The cake debate continues; Erin offers her opinion
jokes.punchline: Erin's case for cupcakes is purely personal vanity — she looks hot eating them — delivered with complete sincerity as if this is a relevant party planning consideration
jokes.explanation: 'I am one of the few people who looks hot eating a cupcake' is a great Erin line — guileless self-admiration as the deciding factor in a professional decision. The sincerity makes it land.

jokes.text: Angela to Pam: 'We don't really care about your opinion. You're just a tie-breaker.'
jokes.setup: Pam has been brought in to adjudicate the cupcake/erotic cake debate
jokes.punchline: Angela bluntly tells Pam her opinion is irrelevant — she's only there as a mathematical tie-breaker, not a valued voice
jokes.explanation: Angela at her most Angela — brutal honesty delivered without any awareness of cruelty. Economy is excellent. Perfect character integration.

jokes.text: Gabe follows Erin into the women's bathroom and Michael says 'Hey, Creed. Not cool, man.' — then Creed is apparently also in the women's bathroom
jokes.setup: Gabe is pursuing Erin into the women's bathroom to profess his love
jokes.punchline: Michael's reproach of 'Creed' — not Gabe — implies Creed was already in the women's bathroom for his own reasons, making him the bigger transgressor by implication
jokes.explanation: The Creed-in-the-women's-bathroom implication is perfect background comedy. The audience has to work it out: Michael is addressing Creed, not Gabe, which means Creed is already in there for unspecified Creed-reasons. The economy of a single 'Hey, Creed. Not cool, man.' implies an entire terrifying scenario. Creed's weirdness is the show's most reliable background joke and this is a perfect deployment.

jokes.text: Gabe: 'Someday, you are going to tell our grandchildren about how their grandfather won you back in a women's room.'
jokes.setup: Gabe is desperately pursuing Erin in the women's bathroom
jokes.punchline: Gabe envisions their grandchildren hearing the romantic story of being won back 'in a women's room' — completely unaware of how un-romantic this scenario is
jokes.explanation: The future-projection to grandchildren is a great cringe escalation — Gabe is so far into his delusion that he's already romanticizing the bathroom confrontation as an epic love story. The specificity of 'grandchildren' and 'women's room' in the same sentence is the joke.

jokes.text: Toby tries to connect Michael with his brother in Boulder: Toby: 'Does he like jams? My shelves are overflowing with preserves.' Michael: 'Well, no, he hates jams.'
jokes.setup: Toby is making a sweet gesture of connecting Michael with his Boulder-based brother
jokes.punchline: Toby's immediate follow-up is offering jam — and Michael casually reveals his brother hates jams, a specific detail that somehow makes Toby's hoarding of preserves sadder and funnier
jokes.explanation: The detail that Toby's shelves are 'overflowing with preserves' and his brother 'hates jams' adds a layer of pathetic Toby-ness. He has all this jam and the one person he knows in Boulder won't want it. Small but effective.

jokes.text: Michael gives Darryl his only copy of 'Somehow I Manage' — a chapter called 'Gum' with one sentence: 'Everybody likes the guy who offers them a stick of gum.'
jokes.setup: Michael presents his unpublished management book manuscript to Darryl as a going-away gift
jokes.punchline: The revealed chapter content — 'Gum.' followed by one sentence of profundity — encapsulates Michael's management philosophy: a single piece of gum wisdom presented as deep insight
jokes.explanation: This is one of the best jokes in the episode. 'Everybody likes the guy who offers them a stick of gum' as the entire content of a management book chapter is perfect Michael Scott comedy — it's not wrong, it's just so shallow it's existentially funny. The setup (a book called 'Somehow I Manage' with chapters) creates the expectation of depth; the payoff is a single gum sentence. The chapter title 'Gum' followed by one sentence achieves maximum comic economy. This is Darryl's reaction face made text, and it would be iconic on any rewatch. Comparable in quality to the anchor examples.

jokes.text: Darryl: 'Mmm-hmm. It's true.' — about the gum sentence
jokes.setup: Darryl has just read the gum sentence from Michael's management book
jokes.punchline: Darryl doesn't laugh or mock it — he genuinely affirms it. 'It's true.' The joke is that the gum advice is both idiotic AND accurate, and Darryl's straightman reaction reveals this perfectly
jokes.explanation: Two words that validate and condemn Michael simultaneously. 'It's true' from Darryl — the most grounded character — means the gum advice actually works, which makes Michael's entire management philosophy both absurd AND functional. Perfect button on the gum joke. Economy is maximal: two words do the work of a full comedic analysis.

jokes.text: Michael asks to use the warehouse baler as his last wish. Darryl says no. Michael says 'Darryl said I could use the baler because I'm leaving.' Darryl: 'No.'
jokes.setup: Michael asks to use the baler as a final wish; Darryl refuses
jokes.punchline: Michael immediately turns around and lies to the warehouse staff that Darryl gave permission — with Darryl standing right there to deny it
jokes.explanation: Michael's immediate pivot to lying — with Darryl right there — is a perfect character beat. His audacity and complete failure to plan a lie that could work is pure Michael. Darryl's single-word 'No.' is a perfect button.

jokes.text: Michael says goodbye to the warehouse workers: 'Catch you on the flippety-flip.' — repeated 5+ times as he can't bring himself to leave
jokes.setup: Michael is saying goodbye to the warehouse; each time he says it, he comes back
jokes.punchline: 'Catch you on the flippety-flip' becomes funnier with each repetition as Michael keeps returning to say it again, unable to actually leave — the phrase itself becoming absurd through sheer repetition
jokes.explanation: The joke escalates with each repetition — 'flippety-flip' is already an absurd phrase, and Michael's inability to actually leave makes it funnier each time. The emotional subtext (he can't say a final goodbye to people he claims he doesn't care about) gives it genuine poignancy. One of the episode's most memorable running gag sequences. The phrase itself is extremely quotable.

jokes.text: Jim's camera look/reaction as the 'flippety-flip' extends beyond all reasonable limits
jokes.setup: Michael has said 'flippety-flip' an absurd number of times and keeps returning
jokes.punchline: Jim's deadpan look to camera expresses what the audience is feeling — this is unbearable and also wonderful
jokes.explanation: Jim's reaction look is economical confirmation of what the audience feels. Not structurally complex, but perfectly placed as a punctuation on the running gag. The show's house style at work.

jokes.text: Michael's sales pitch approach with Andy: 'Okay, what's our approach? You a veteran? Do I have a month to live? You gonna get married tomorrow?' Andy: 'I thought we'd just talk about our customer service and exceptional paper quality.'
jokes.setup: Michael and Andy are heading to a client meeting; Andy has a normal approach prepared
jokes.punchline: Michael's 'approach' suggestions are all manipulative emotional scenarios (dying, veteran status, imminent wedding) — sympathy plays rather than actual sales. Andy's straight response about paper quality is the deadpan foil.
jokes.explanation: Michael's entire sales philosophy exposed in one quick exchange — he sells through emotional manipulation rather than product knowledge. Andy's 'exceptional paper quality' response is the perfect naive foil. Good structure with Andy's straight-man reaction landing the joke.

jokes.text: Michael: 'That's stupid. Well, what do I know? I know. What do you know?'
jokes.setup: Andy suggests talking about paper quality to their client
jokes.punchline: Michael's rapid self-contradiction — calling Andy's idea stupid, then immediately undermining himself, then re-asserting — is a perfect portrait of his erratic thought process
jokes.explanation: Short character beat showing Michael's rapid intellectual incoherence. Functional character comedy.

jokes.text: Michael, looking for a way to 'get psyched up': 'Is there an animal shelter on the way?' Andy: 'Yeah.' Michael: 'Awesome! Ani-ani-shelto. Here we come.'
jokes.setup: Michael wants to get psyched up for the sales call and asks about nearby animal shelters
jokes.punchline: 'Ani-ani-shelto. Here we come.' — Michael has coined a battle cry for visiting an animal shelter as pre-meeting motivation, including a nonsense portmanteau of the destination
jokes.explanation: 'Ani-ani-shelto' as a battle cry is gloriously Michael — the enthusiasm is there, the coherence is not. The non-sequitur of an animal shelter as pre-sales motivation is perfectly absurd, and the made-up word lands as a confident nonsense rallying cry.

jokes.text: Andy: 'Do you know how to high-five?' Michael: 'Yeah.' Andy: 'Cause if you do, now's the time.' Michael: '...Not while I'm driving.'
jokes.setup: Andy is getting hyped up for the sales call and wants to high-five
jokes.punchline: Michael's response: 'Not while I'm driving' — he agrees in principle, just has a safety objection to the timing
jokes.explanation: The structure is clean: Andy sets up an urgent, enthusiastic invitation; Michael deflates it with a calm practical objection. The 'not while I'm driving' takes the wind entirely out of the hype sails.

jokes.text: Deangelo's story of how he got his job: 'Walking along, out of work, again... I see this guy trying to steal this lady's dog. So I grab the dog, he runs off. She's so grateful, she hires me.' — then he re-enacts it dramatically with Michael
jokes.setup: Deangelo tells Michael his origin story of meeting Jo Bennett and getting hired
jokes.punchline: Deangelo not only tells the story but immediately re-enacts it with Michael playing the dog thief — with full physical commitment: 'Gimme that dog! It's not your dog!'
jokes.explanation: The story itself is funny (getting hired for heroic dog rescue), but the escalation to physically re-enacting it with Michael — with full intensity, 'Don't ever do it again!' — is the real joke. Deangelo's total commitment to the bit and Michael's confused but willing participation is great character comedy. The 'Do you feel that energy?' button lands it.

jokes.text: Erin, on choosing between Gabe and Andy: 'I wish I knew who my birth mother was so she could just tell me who to choose.'
jokes.setup: Erin is asking for advice on her love life — choosing between Gabe and Andy
jokes.punchline: Erin's solution is to consult her birth mother — whom she's never met — treating a stranger's opinion as the definitive authority on her romantic life
jokes.explanation: This is a great Erin line — her foster care background is always played with a light touch on the show, and this joke takes her genuine vulnerability (not knowing her birth mother) and channels it into an absurd romantic logic. Only Erin would think 'I need my birth mother's opinion on this.' The dark undertone (she genuinely doesn't know her) and the comic framing (as if birth mother = romantic oracle) are perfectly balanced. High character integration.

jokes.text: Kevin walks by; Erin: 'Kevin?' / Kevin: 'Andy.' — Erin mistook Kevin for a romantic option
jokes.setup: Erin mentions she's in love with 'someone else' and Andy assumes she means him
jokes.punchline: Erin glances at Kevin passing by, Andy says 'Kevin?' and Erin clarifies 'Andy' — but the moment of ambiguity implies she actually considered Kevin as an option
jokes.explanation: Quick misdirection that implies Erin might have briefly considered Kevin — the look toward Kevin and Andy's 'Kevin?' is a fast, efficient joke. Economy is strong.

jokes.text: Andy gives Erin a heartfelt speech ending with: 'you are beautiful, and you are fun, and you are smart... you don't need a mom, because you have my number and you can call me anytime. Extension 147.'
jokes.setup: Andy gives Erin genuine, warm advice about not rushing into a relationship
jokes.punchline: Andy's sweet 'you don't need a mom' callback to Erin's birth mother comment is immediately undermined by him giving her his office extension number — turning an emotional moment into an awkward self-referential offer
jokes.explanation: The 'extension 147' at the end is a perfect Office-style deflation of an earnest moment. Andy means it well, but giving a girl your office extension as a substitute for maternal connection is tonally hilarious. The show's ability to make cringe and sweetness coexist is on display.

jokes.text: Michael calls an emergency conference meeting to ask about (1) Pam's whereabouts, and (2) whether Phyllis has finished his mittens
jokes.setup: Michael calls everyone into the conference room on his last day for what seems like an important announcement
jokes.punchline: The two urgent agenda items are: where is Pam, and are his mittens done — not a meaningful goodbye speech, just logistics and handknits
jokes.explanation: The comedy is the gap between the gravitas of Michael's 'last conference room meeting ever' and the utter triviality of his two agenda items. He gathered the whole office to ask about mittens. The structure mirrors the episode's emotional arc — Michael can't actually confront the goodbye, so he hides behind logistics. High character integration.

jokes.text: Dwight reads Michael's letter of recommendation aloud: 'To whom it may concern.' Then: 'The dictionary defines superlative as...' Dwight: 'If I wanted the dictionary definition, I'd buy a dictionary.'
jokes.setup: Michael presents Dwight with a letter of recommendation he wrote for him.
jokes.punchline: The letter opens with 'To whom it may concern' (hilariously impersonal for a personal favor) and immediately pivots to a dictionary definition — which Dwight correctly identifies as the worst recommendation letter opening possible.
jokes.explanation: 'To whom it may concern' — 'real personal, thanks Michael' — is excellent structure. Then the dictionary definition punchline builds on it, and Dwight's deadpan 'if I wanted the dictionary definition I'd buy a dictionary' is the payoff. The joke works because both the letter's failings are real recommendation letter clichés that Dwight (and the audience) recognizes immediately. Good craft.

jokes.text: Dwight reads 'Lots more like that. Really repetitive.' — a note apparently written in the letter itself acknowledging its own repetitiveness.
jokes.setup: Dwight is reading the letter of recommendation aloud.
jokes.punchline: The letter apparently contains a self-aware annotation — 'Lots more like that. Really repetitive.' — either written by Michael as a genuine note or Dwight's own editorial on the letter.
jokes.explanation: Ambiguous but funny either way — if Michael wrote it, it's a perfectly Michael piece of self-awareness; if Dwight said it, it's a rare Dwight reading moment. The self-referential quality ('really repetitive') in a recommendation letter is the joke.

jokes.text: The paintball sequence — Michael and Dwight shooting at each other, laughing, Dwight takes a hit ('Ow!') — pure physical comedy joy inferred from the action markers.
jokes.setup: Michael has secretly arranged a final paintball battle with Dwight.
jokes.punchline: The sheer delight of the sequence — two grown men in a parking lot shooting each other as a goodbye — is its own punchline. Dwight's 'Ow!' suggests he takes a hit but continues.
jokes.explanation: The sequence earns its emotional/comedic impact from the setup (joke #56). As a standalone visual joke it's strong but relies on the context. The 'Ow!' mid-battle is perfect Dwight — he registers pain but would never stop. Rewatch bonus is high.

jokes.text: Michael's rapid-fire triple goodbye: 'Whether you're scared of dying, or dying alone, or dying drunk in a ditch, don't be. It's going to be okay.'
jokes.setup: Michael is trying to have meaningful individual goodbye moments with everyone
jokes.punchline: 'Dying drunk in a ditch' as one of the three universal fears Michael addresses in his goodbye — the escalation from generic fears to this specific grim image is the joke
jokes.explanation: The three-part escalation (dying → dying alone → dying drunk in a ditch) is structurally clean, and 'drunk in a ditch' is a specific Meredith-level image that feels targeted while being delivered as universal comfort. Michael's confidence that 'it's going to be okay' whatever the ditch scenario completes the absurdist comfort.

jokes.text: Michael to Gabe: 'A little cover-up on your Adam's apple will make it appear smaller, which will make you look less like a transvestite.'
jokes.setup: Gabe is spiraling over Erin's rejection; Michael offers advice
jokes.punchline: Michael's 'advice' is cosmetic tips targeting Gabe's prominent Adam's apple — the specific, personal nature of the insult disguised as helpful guidance
jokes.explanation: Michael's casual cruelty-as-kindness targeting Gabe's insecurity is effective cringe comedy. The specific targeting of the Adam's apple — a real Gabe physical feature — and the transvestite comment is harsh. Lower on earned-vs-cheap because it's primarily an appearance-based insult dressed as advice rather than structural wit.

jokes.text: Jim's reaction: 'That is cold, sir. Absolutely cold.' — then: 'It was a complete waste of my time.' (about his visit to the client with Michael)
jokes.setup: Michael has just insulted Gabe's appearance; then apparently tanked a client meeting
jokes.punchline: Jim's moral reaction to Michael's Gabe advice ('cold, sir'), contrasted with his pragmatic assessment of what Michael did to the client visit — the two responses revealing Jim's priority ordering
jokes.explanation: Jim's 'cold, sir' is a good straight-man button. The pivot to 'complete waste of my time' reveals what Jim actually cared about. Functional.

jokes.text: Deangelo apologizes for Michael's behavior at the client meeting: 'I could tell you that he has a steel plate in his head, or that he's crazy, but the truth is, I think he's just a terrible salesman.'
jokes.setup: Deangelo is cleaning up after Michael apparently sabotaged the client meeting
jokes.punchline: 'The truth is, I think he's just a terrible salesman' — Deangelo rejects the sympathetic excuses (medical, mental) in favor of the plainest possible professional assessment
jokes.explanation: Great deadpan structure: offer generous excuses (steel plate, crazy), then cut to the brutal truth. The client staying anyway ('Keep talking') makes it the ultimate Deangelo save. 'I think he's just a terrible salesman' delivered as a confession is perfect.

jokes.text: Michael: 'Power through the arthritis, Phyllis. You can do it.'
jokes.setup: Phyllis explains her knuckles are swelling and she can't finish knitting
jokes.punchline: Michael's response to an elderly woman's arthritis pain is 'power through it' — with cheerful encouragement, no awareness of how callous this is
jokes.explanation: 'Power through the arthritis' is a great cringe line — Michael's relentless optimism deployed in a context where someone is in physical pain. His cheerful disregard for the medical reality is pure character.

jokes.text: Michael introduces 'Ping' — his offensive Asian character — to the whole office as a 'special guest' farewell
jokes.setup: Michael promises a special guest for the going-away party
jokes.punchline: Michael himself appears doing 'Ping,' a racist caricature of an Asian person, complete with accent ('I rove you'), performing it as a sincere farewell tribute
jokes.explanation: This is where the show's cringe formula gets genuinely uncomfortable in ways that haven't aged well. Michael's racism is always the joke (we laugh at Michael, not with him), and the show knows Ping is offensive — that IS the joke about Michael's obliviousness. But the 'earned vs. cheap' score suffers because the cringe here crosses into discomfort without enough structural payoff. The office's reaction (muted disgust) is the real punchline. Scored lower than similar moments because the craft relies primarily on audience discomfort rather than wit.

jokes.text: Jim tells Michael he wants to take him out for lunch tomorrow — his last day. Then catches himself: 'You're not leaving tomorrow. You're leaving today, right?'
jokes.setup: Jim invites Michael to lunch tomorrow for his last day.
jokes.punchline: Jim realizes mid-invitation that Michael is leaving today — 'you're not leaving tomorrow, you're leaving today, right?' The moment is a small comedy of manners as Jim catches the deception.
jokes.explanation: This is a transitional joke before the emotional climax. Jim's gentle calling-out of Michael's lie is understated and real. The rewatch bonus is significant — knowing this is Jim and Michael's real goodbye makes the comedic beats here hit harder.

jokes.text: Michael: 'T-shirt idea. Goodbyes stink.'
jokes.setup: Jim has just told Michael that 'sometimes goodbyes are a bitch'
jokes.punchline: Michael immediately brain-files it as a T-shirt slogan — his mind is perpetually in entrepreneurial mode even in emotional moments
jokes.explanation: Quintessential Michael. An emotionally resonant Jim moment about goodbyes is immediately converted by Michael into a product concept. 'T-shirt idea' as a category he maintains — with the instant filing of 'Goodbyes stink' — reveals his brain is always running a parallel track of entrepreneurship. Maximum economy, perfect character integration, highly quotable. One of the episode's best lines.

jokes.text: Michael begins a formal, emotional goodbye to Jim ('James Halpert... you started with this company as a fine young man') — Jim cuts it off: 'I think we should just save the goodbyes for tomorrow. At lunch.'
jokes.setup: Michael launches into his big formal goodbye speech to Jim
jokes.punchline: Jim interrupts — not because he doesn't care, but because he knows Michael is actually leaving TODAY, and this is Jim's way of letting Michael off the hook from the false 'tomorrow' plan while giving them both an exit
jokes.explanation: The comedy and the emotion are perfectly fused here. Jim's interruption is both funny (stopping a Michael speech mid-wind) and deeply kind (giving Michael an out). The 'best boss I ever had' reveal — that this IS Jim's goodbye — lands as both a laugh and a gut punch. The joke is structurally the interrupted speech; the heart is what Jim says instead.

jokes.text: Jim confessional after Michael leaves: 'Best boss I ever had.'
jokes.setup: Jim has just said goodbye to Michael with a gentle lie about 'lunch tomorrow'
jokes.punchline: 'Best boss I ever had' — delivered to camera with Jim's trademark sincerity/irony blend; in context, it's meant completely sincerely, which is the ultimate irony given seven seasons of Michael's behavior
jokes.explanation: Four words that carry seven seasons of relationship. The joke — if it is a joke — is that Jim means it. After everything Michael has done, all the cringe and embarrassment and bad management, Jim's honest assessment is 'best boss I ever had.' The economy is perfect: no setup needed, no punchline, just the weight of the line against the history. This sits at the edge of comedy and genuine emotion, which is where The Office lives at its best. It would get 9.5 impact in a room — not from laughter, but from the collective recognition of something true. The craft score reflects the structural perfection of ending a multi-act comedy episode on this.

jokes.text: Michael finds Phyllis still knitting his unfinished mittens; she says 'Oh, they're still not done.' Michael examines them: 'Nice try. I love them.'
jokes.setup: Michael has been waiting all episode for Phyllis to finish his mittens before he leaves
jokes.punchline: The mittens are clearly terrible and unfinished; Michael examines them, says 'Nice try' (acknowledging their inadequacy) then immediately declares 'I love them' — accepting failure as a gift
jokes.explanation: 'Nice try. I love them.' is a perfect button on the mitten subplot — Michael's 'nice try' reveals he knows they're bad, but his immediate pivot to 'I love them' shows his genuine warmth. The joke earns a higher score for being both funny and genuinely moving as a character beat. He takes the bad mittens because Phyllis tried.

jokes.text: Michael's final confessional: 'The people that you work with are just, when you get down to it, your very best friends.' — followed by: 'I actually don't understand deathbeds. I mean, who would buy that?'
jokes.setup: Michael delivers a genuinely moving final thought about work and friendship
jokes.punchline: He pivots from moving philosophy to literal confusion about deathbed furniture economics — completely undercutting the sentiment with his signature obliviousness
jokes.explanation: This is a masterclass in The Office's tonal balance. Michael says something genuinely profound about friendship, then immediately reveals he takes the 'deathbed' expression literally and is confused by the furniture market. 'Who would buy that?' — Michael Scott, questioning the business model of end-of-life furniture, in the middle of his farewell. The structure (profound → absurd) is clean, the character integration is maximal, and the final confusion grounds the whole emotional moment.

jokes.text: Michael removes his microphone pack: 'This is gonna feel so good getting this thing off my chest.' Then, beat. 'That's what she said.'
jokes.setup: Michael is removing his documentary microphone on his last day — a genuinely symbolic act
jokes.punchline: Michael pauses, then cannot help himself: 'That's what she said.' — his most signature joke, deployed one final time
jokes.explanation: The single best joke in the episode and one of the best jokes in the series' run. This is the show at its absolute peak. The structure is impeccable: the microphone removal is genuinely moving (he's stepping out of the documentary, out of our lives), the setup line 'this is gonna feel so good getting this thing off my chest' is perfect (unintentionally innuendo-laden), the pause gives the audience a moment to feel the weight — and then Michael cannot let his final act be something other than himself. The 'That's what she said' is simultaneously his most Michael moment ever and the perfect comedic goodbye. It's funny, it's emotional, and it's completely true to who Michael Scott is: a man who experiences life through jokes. The craft scores are near-perfect: only this character, only this moment, only these words. Among the best final jokes a character has ever delivered in a sitcom. This is what a 9-10 looks like.

jokes.text: Pam's airport scene — entirely visual/implied from Dwight's report: she ran to the airport to say goodbye, and we learn 'he was full of hope... hoping to get an upgrade as an awards member... excited to see Holly'
jokes.setup: The office learns Pam ran to the airport to say goodbye to Michael
jokes.punchline: Dwight's report undercuts the grand romantic gesture by listing Michael's mundane airport concerns (upgrade, awards membership) alongside 'seeing Holly' — Michael's actual last-minute concerns are completely practical
jokes.explanation: The joke of Michael's airport concerns being 'upgrade as awards member' alongside 'see Holly' is perfect Michael — he's equally excited about frequent flyer status and the love of his life. Dwight's flat delivery of this report is the deadpan vehicle. Works emotionally (Pam did something beautiful) and comedically (Michael wanted an upgrade) simultaneously.

jokes.text: Deangelo: 'Well, if he's not gonna make it, at least we should go ahead and eat the cake.' — then aggressively eats cake, then self-recrimination spiral
jokes.setup: The office is processing Michael's departure; Deangelo is the new manager
jokes.punchline: Deangelo is revealed as someone with a compulsive relationship with cake — he eats aggressively, then says 'This is not even that good. I don't even want it.' then 'I had cake for lunch.' then 'No, you know what? I've been good. I deserve this.' — a complete compulsion loop
jokes.explanation: The cake spiral is a brilliant piece of character introduction/escalation for Deangelo. Each beat reveals more — he eats without wanting to, he rationalizes, he self-condemns, he re-rationalizes ('I deserve this'). The closing 'No! Uh-oh. No!' suggests he's having a full breakdown over cake. It's a funny closing tag that also seeds Deangelo's character for the episodes ahead.

tmdb_overview: Michael wants to have a drama-free day at work on his last day before moving to Colorado. Meanwhile, Deangelo Vickers and Andy Bernard scramble to retain Michael's biggest clients.
